case_study_insert.main_stem: Bramblewick Creamery (BRW) is a cooperative in the dairy-processing sector, employing a workforce of 64. Founded in 2003 by farmer Nora Bramblewick, it produces yoghurts and fresh cream for supermarkets and independent delis and operates a flat organisational structure with laissez-faire leadership. BRW plans to invest $910,000 in a new yoghurt filling line with returnable glass jars, financed by a $560,000 ten-year bank loan and $350,000 hire purchase. It has fixed costs of $242,000 a year, a variable cost of $6.80 a unit and a selling price of $12.30, and currently produces 95,000 units a year. BRW faces two problems: labour turnover is rising and product waste has reached 5%.
case_study_insert.appendix_1_marketing_ops: Quality and Waste Report — Q4 2025: The filling line produced 24,000 pots last month at a defect rate of 2.7%, down from 4.0% a year ago. Customer complaints fell from 52 to 30 per month. Average delivery time is 3.6 days. A survey of 520 shoppers found that 66% preferred returnable glass jars and 57% would pay up to $0.45 more for them. A training review shows 18 of 64 staff need on-the-job training on the new filler; an off-the-job course at the college costs $780 per employee.

appendix_2_financial_data.title: Extract from the Statement of Financial Position of Bramblewick Creamery as at 31 March 2025 ($ '000)

case_study_insert.appendix_3_external_environment: Economic and Business Bulletin (January 2027): (1) The central bank cut the base interest rate from 5.25% to 4.75%, reducing borrowing costs on BRW's variable-rate loan. (2) The national minimum wage will rise by 6.1% from $13.80 to $14.64 per hour from April 2026, raising wage costs. (3) Wholesale milk and glass input costs have risen 10.5% year-on-year, and dairy-product inflation is 6.8%, while consumer spending on yoghurt grew 3.1%.

questions.question_text: BRW funds part of its filling-line expansion with a $560,000 bank loan. Explain two advantages for BRW of using hire purchase instead of the bank loan.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Hire purchase spreads the cost of the $350,000 filling equipment over regular payments, so BRW does not need to service the full $560,000 bank loan immediately and preserves cash for the cooperative's 64 members and its $242,000 a year of fixed costs. The equipment is used to generate output while it is paid for, helping fund the 95,000-unit plan.

Point 2: Hire purchase is secured on the specific asset, so it can be easier to arrange than a large unsecured loan and does not require BRW to pledge other dairy assets. With the base rate having fallen to 4.75%, financing costs are also contained. This leaves more of the cooperative's resources free to absorb the 10.5% rise in milk and glass input costs without immediately raising the $12.30 selling price for supermarkets and delis.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid point identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation linked to BRW's financing, costs and output.

questions.question_text: BRW is relaunching its yoghurt range in returnable glass jars. Consider national television advertising, in-store supermarket demonstrations, or social media influencer marketing. Which should BRW choose? Justify your recommendation.
questions.model_answer:
National television advertising: TV would build awareness of the returnable-glass-jar yoghurts across all the supermarkets stocking BRW. However, airtime is costly for a 64-member cooperative funding a $910,000 filling line, and much of the audience is outside the deli and supermarket catchment, so the spend would be poorly converted into pots sold.

In-store supermarket demonstrations: Tastings let shoppers try the product and learn how returnable glass jars work, directly reaching buyers at the point of purchase and supporting the 24,000 pots produced monthly. They can also explain the 2.7% defect-rate improvement. Drawbacks are high staff time, limited geographic coverage and dependence on supermarket permission, which may be hard to secure across every chain.

Social media influencer marketing: Food and family influencers can target precisely the 66% of 520 surveyed shoppers who prefer returnable glass jars and the 57% who would pay up to $0.45 more, showing the jars and the return process in short videos. Engagement is measurable and cost per contact low. Results build more slowly than TV and rely on influencer credibility, but the research fit is strongest and the message scales nationally.

Recommendation: BRW should choose social media influencer marketing. It reaches the research-identified shoppers who value returnable glass jars, costs far less than television and scales beyond the few stores covered by demonstrations, while supporting the $12.30 price. Television is rejected as expensive and untargeted for a cooperative spending $910,000; in-store demonstrations are rejected as labour-intensive and too narrow, though a few can be used to support the launch.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Identifies promotional options with limited reference to BRW.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Discusses advantages and disadvantages of at least two options in BRW's context with some judgement.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Discusses all three options in BRW's context and recommends influencer marketing with clear reasons for rejecting television and demonstrations.

questions.question_text: BRW's labour turnover is rising and product waste has reached 5%. Explain two benefits for BRW of using laissez-faire leadership to improve motivation on the filling line.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Laissez-faire leadership gives BRW's 64 cooperative members and experienced filler operators freedom to decide how to organise their work, which can raise intrinsic motivation and job satisfaction. In a flat structure this suits skilled staff who want autonomy, helping to slow the rising labour turnover without adding management layers.

Point 2: Allowing operators to suggest and implement their own improvements can reduce the 5% product waste and sustain the 2.7% defect rate, because the people closest to the filler understand the causes better than distant managers. Lower waste protects the $5.50 contribution per unit and the 95,000-unit output. The $780 off-the-job training budget can then be focused on the 18 staff still needing skills, rather than on supervising motivated workers.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid point identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for development linked to BRW's turnover, waste, defect rate and training.

questions.question_text: BRW must train 18 staff on the new filler. Consider on-the-job training or off-the-job training at the college. Which should BRW choose? Justify your decision.
questions.model_answer:
On-the-job training: Coaching at the filler teaches BRW's exact machine settings and quality checks, costs no fees, and keeps the 18 staff productive while learning, protecting the 24,000-pot monthly output and the fall in defect rate to 2.7%. Weaknesses are that mentors are operators whose own work suffers, bad habits can spread, and there is no certificate that supermarket auditors might expect.

Off-the-job training: The college course at $780 per employee delivers structured, up-to-date skills and a recognised qualification for all 18 staff, costing $14,040 — manageable against the $910,000 investment. It removes staff from the line when waste is already 5%, reducing short-term capacity, and generic content may not match BRW's filler, so on-site follow-up would still be needed.

Decision: BRW should choose on-the-job training as the main method, with short college courses for a few lead operators. It is cheaper, machine-specific and avoids output loss while waste is 5% and turnover rising; full off-the-job training is rejected because $14,040 and eighteen absences would disrupt supermarket and deli deliveries, and the course can be added once the filler is stable and the 18 staff have hands-on competence.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Describes the two training methods with limited application to BRW.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analyses benefits and drawbacks of one or both methods in BRW's context.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Evaluates both methods in BRW's context with a justified decision covering cost, disruption and machine relevance.

questions.question_text: Calculate and explain how BRW's management can use its cost, break-even and productivity data.
questions.model_answer: (i) Break-even output = 44,000 units | (ii) Contribution per unit = $5.50 | (iii) Four contextual uses: margin of safety against 95,000-unit output; pricing against $242,000 fixed costs; loan and hire-purchase affordability for the $910,000 line; and unit-cost benchmarking at $9.35 to reduce 5% waste.

working_marks: 1 mark for correct formula and 1 mark for the accurate answer in each calculation; 1 mark per valid applied use in (iii).

sub_parts.model_answer: Formula: Break-even output = Fixed costs ÷ Contribution per unit. Substitution: $242,000 ÷ ($12.30 − $6.80) = $242,000 ÷ $5.50 = 44,000 units. Answer: break-even output is 44,000 units a year.
Formula: Contribution per unit = Selling price − Variable cost per unit. Substitution: $12.30 − $6.80 = $5.50. Answer: contribution per unit is $5.50.

sub_parts.question_text: Explain four ways BRW's management can use this financial data.
sub_parts.model_answer:
1. Managers can compare the 44,000-unit break-even output with actual output of 95,000 units, a margin of safety of 51,000 units, to see how far demand for yoghurt could fall before the new line loses money.
2. Contribution per unit of $5.50 lets BRW test a supermarket price cut: a $0.45 discount would leave $5.05, showing the extra volume needed to cover $242,000 of fixed costs.
3. Knowing contribution and fixed costs helps check that 95,000 units generate enough to meet the $560,000 bank loan and $350,000 hire-purchase payments, supporting the $910,000 investment decision.
4. Unit cost of $9.35 ($242,000 ÷ 95,000 units + $6.80) gives a benchmark to isolate the 5% product waste and 2.7% defect rate, guiding supplier talks amid 10.5% milk and glass inflation.

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 2, evaluate BRW's financial position by calculating the current ratio and the acid test ratio for 2024 and 2025. Has BRW's financial position improved? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Calculations:
Current Ratio 2024 = 1.30 : 1
Current Ratio 2025 = 1.40 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2024 = 0.85 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2025 = 0.98 : 1

Detailed workings: 2024 current assets = $90,000 inventories + $125,000 trade receivables + $45,000 cash = $260,000; 2025 current assets = $80,000 + $136,000 + $50,000 = $266,000. Dividing by current liabilities of $200,000 and $190,000 gives 1.30 and 1.40. Excluding inventories, $170,000 ÷ $200,000 = 0.85 in 2024 and $186,000 ÷ $190,000 = 0.98 in 2025.

Evaluation: Liquidity has improved. The broader measure rose from 1.30 to 1.40 because current liabilities fell from $200,000 to $190,000 while current assets edged up to $266,000. The stricter measure improved from 0.85 to 0.98, helped by inventories falling from $90,000 to $80,000, so BRW relies less on selling stock to meet short-term debts — valuable while it services a $560,000 bank loan and $350,000 hire purchase. However, trade receivables rose from $125,000 to $136,000, tying up cash, and the stricter measure is still just below 1, so a squeeze on supermarket payments could quickly weaken the position.

Conclusion: BRW's financial position has improved. Both measures are higher and the stricter measure moved closer to full coverage without depending on inventories. The remaining risk is rising receivables, so the cooperative should tighten credit control before committing further funds to the $910,000 filling line.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: States figures with little or no accurate calculation.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Calculates both ratios for both years accurately with some contextual analysis.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Accurate calculations plus detailed evaluation of inventories, receivables and liabilities and a justified conclusion.

questions.question_text: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for BRW of using returnable glass jars for its yoghurt range.
questions.model_answer:
Advantage: Returnable glass jars match the 66% of 520 surveyed shoppers who prefer them and the 57% who would pay up to $0.45 more, allowing BRW to defend the $5.50 contribution per unit as 10.5% milk and glass input costs rise. The positioning also helps it keep listings with supermarkets and independent delis for the $910,000 filling line.

Disadvantage: Returnable glass is heavier and more fragile than plastic pots, which could raise the $6.80 variable cost per unit through delivery and washing, and worsen the 5% product waste and 2.7% defect rate if jars chip. Unless the full $0.45 premium is achieved across the range, the extra cost would squeeze margins on the 95,000-unit output.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid point identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual development using BRW's research, costs and waste data.

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the interest rate cut to 4.75%, the 6.1% minimum wage increase and the 10.5% rise in input costs will affect BRW. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Interest rate cut (5.25% to 4.75%): This is beneficial for BRW because the insert records a $560,000 variable-rate bank loan. If that loan tracks the base rate, a 0.50% fall saves 0.50% × $560,000 = $2,800 a year (0.005 × $560,000), easing the burden alongside $242,000 of fixed costs. It also makes the $350,000 hire purchase or future borrowing cheaper and may support consumer spending on yoghurt, but the saving is modest and depends on the loan actually being variable-rate.

Minimum wage increase (6.1%, to $14.64 per hour): With a workforce of 64 in filling and packing, this raises BRW's wage bill and cannot be avoided. The insert gives no hours worked or individual pay, so no annual total can be invented; the defensible comparison is productivity — 95,000 units ÷ 64 staff is about 1,484 units per worker, so the rise is bearable only if that productivity holds or output grows, otherwise unit labour cost erodes the $5.50 contribution.

Input cost inflation (10.5% milk and glass): The insert never decomposes the $6.80 variable cost, so only a bound is honest — if the whole variable cost rose 10.5% it would add 10.5% × $6.80 = $0.71 per unit, and at 95,000 units that is about $67,900 a year. Even a partial pass-through would cut contribution, and 6.8% dairy-product inflation may limit BRW's ability to raise price to supermarkets.

Conclusion: The 10.5% input-cost rise will have the greatest impact. It repeats on every one of the 95,000 units and directly erodes the contribution behind the $910,000 line, while the interest cut is a benefit worth only about $2,800 and the wage rise can partly be offset by productivity.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the three external changes with limited application to BRW.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two changes on BRW's costs, financing or revenue in context.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Evaluates all three changes with a justified judgment that input-cost inflation has the greatest impact and why the others are smaller.
